stem: Hydrocarbon X contains 85.7% carbon and 14.3% hydrogen by mass. Its relative molecular mass is 56. X decolorises bromine water at room temperature. When X is heated with concentrated, acidified potassium manganate(VII), ethanoic acid is the only organic product. Data: Ar C = 12.0, H = 1.0.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the empirical formula of X (type it, for example CH3).

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Deduce the molecular formula of X.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: How many alkenes have the formula of X? Count cis and trans isomers separately.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Use the reaction with manganate(VII) to identify X, explaining your reasoning.

points.description: Each =CHCH₃ end of a C=C is oxidised to CH₃COOH
Only ethanoic acid forms, so both ends are =CHCH₃: X is CH₃CH=CHCH₃
X is but-2-ene (but-1-ene would give propanoic acid and CO₂; 2-methylpropene would give propanone and CO₂)

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Hot concentrated manganate(VII) splits the C=C and oxidises each =CHR end to RCOOH. Since ethanoic acid is the only product, each end must be =CHCH₃, so X is CH₃CH=CHCH₃, but-2-ene. But-1-ene would give propanoic acid and carbon dioxide, and 2-methylpropene would give propanone and carbon dioxide.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Explain why X exists as two stereoisomers.

points.description: Restricted rotation about the C=C bond (because of the π bond)
Each carbon of the C=C carries two different groups (H and CH₃), so cis and trans forms exist

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The π bond prevents rotation about the C=C, and each double-bond carbon bears H and CH₃, so the methyl groups can be on the same side (cis) or opposite sides (trans).

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: Which compound with the same molecular formula as X does not decolorise bromine water at room temperature?

options.content: cyclobutane
but-1-ene
2-methylpropene
cis-but-2-ene

parts.label: (g)
parts.stem: Name the alkene that is a chain isomer of X.

explanation: X = but-2-ene, C₄H₈ (empirical CH₂); four alkenes of formula C₄H₈; cis/trans from restricted rotation.
hints: Divide by Ar, then by the smallest.
Each end of the C=C gives one product.

stem: Propane is a component of liquefied petroleum gas. It reacts with chlorine to form a mixture that includes 1-chloropropane and 2-chloropropane.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: State the condition needed for propane to react with chlorine.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Give the equations for the initiation step and for the two propagation steps that form 2-chloropropane.

points.description: Initiation: Cl₂ → 2Cl•
Cl• + CH₃CH₂CH₃ → HCl + CH₃C•HCH₃
CH₃C•HCH₃ + Cl₂ → CH₃CHClCH₃ + Cl•

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Cl₂ → 2Cl•; Cl• + CH₃CH₂CH₃ → HCl + CH₃ĊHCH₃; CH₃ĊHCH₃ + Cl₂ → CH₃CHClCH₃ + Cl•

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Write an equation for a termination step that forms a hydrocarbon with six carbon atoms.

points.description: e.g. 2CH₃CH₂CH₂• → C₆H₁₄, or 2(CH₃)₂CH• → C₆H₁₄, or CH₃CH₂CH₂• + (CH₃)₂CH• → C₆H₁₄

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Why is propane unreactive towards most reagents?

options.content: Its molecules are held together by hydrogen bonds.
options.rationale: Propane has no hydrogen bonding; intermolecular forces do not decide reactivity.

options.content: All of its bonds are strong and almost non-polar.
options.rationale: Correct: no δ+ or δ− sites, and the bonds need much energy to break.

options.content: It has lone pairs that repel electrophiles and nucleophiles.
options.rationale: Carbon in propane has no lone pairs.

options.content: It is a gas, so it cannot collide with other molecules.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Calculate the volume of oxygen, in dm³ at room conditions, needed to burn 0.880 g of propane completely. Ar: C 12.0, H 1.0; molar gas volume 24.0 dm³ mol⁻¹.
parts.explanation: C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O; n(C₃H₈) = 0.880 ÷ 44.0 = 0.0200 mol; n(O₂) = 0.100 mol; V = 2.40 dm³.
parts.workedSolution: 1. C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O; n(C₃H₈) = 0.880 ÷ 44.0 = 0.0200 mol; n(O₂) = 0.100 mol; V = 2.40 dm³.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: How many structural isomers of C₃H₆Cl₂ could form if substitution continues?

parts.label: (g)
parts.stem: Using a large excess of propane increases the proportion of monochlorinated products.
parts.explanation: Cl• then meets propane rather than chloropropane.

explanation: UV; Cl₂ → 2Cl•, then H abstraction and Cl transfer; termination gives C₆H₁₄; 2.40 dm³ O₂.

stem: 1-bromobutane, CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂Br, is a primary halogenoalkane. In one experiment 6.85 g of 1-bromobutane was converted into 2.96 g of pure butan-1-ol.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Which reagent and conditions convert 1-bromobutane into butan-1-ol?

options.content: NaOH in ethanol, heat under reflux
KCN in ethanol, heat under reflux
NaOH(aq), heat under reflux
concentrated H₂SO₄, heat
options.rationale: This does not convert RBr into ROH.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Describe the mechanism of this reaction.

points.description: C–Br polar (C δ+); arrow from a lone pair on O of OH⁻ to the δ+ carbon, attacking opposite Br
Arrow from the C–Br bond to Br
Transition state with partial C–O and C–Br bonds and a negative charge; Br⁻ leaves (SN2)

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The C–Br bond is polar with C δ+. The OH⁻ ion attacks this carbon from the side opposite the bromine (arrow from an O lone pair to C) while the C–Br bonding pair moves onto Br (second arrow). A negatively charged transition state with partial C···O and C···Br bonds forms; then Br⁻ leaves and butan-1-ol forms. This is SN2.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the percentage yield, to one decimal place. Ar: H 1.0, C 12.0, O 16.0, Br 79.9.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Name the organic product when 1-bromobutane is heated with KCN in ethanol.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Give the rate equation for the reaction in (b).
parts.explanation: SN2: first order in each reactant.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: 1-iodobutane is hydrolysed faster than 1-bromobutane. Explain why.

points.description: The C–I bond is weaker (lower bond energy) than C–Br
So it breaks more easily; bond strength, not polarity (C–Br is more polar), controls the rate

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The C–I bond has a lower bond energy than C–Br, so it is broken more easily in the substitution, even though it is less polar.

explanation: NaOH(aq), reflux; SN2; yield 79.9%; KCN gives pentanenitrile; rate = k[RBr][OH⁻]; C–I weakest.

stem: Benzene is nitrated with a mixture of concentrated nitric acid and concentrated sulfuric acid at 50 °C. In one preparation, 5.85 g of benzene gave 6.52 g of nitrobenzene.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Give the formula of the electrophile.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Write an equation for the formation of the electrophile.

points.description: HNO₃ + 2H₂SO₄ → NO₂⁺ + H₃O⁺ + 2HSO₄⁻ (or HNO₃ + H₂SO₄ → NO₂⁺ + HSO₄⁻ + H₂O)

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Describe the mechanism of the reaction of the electrophile with benzene.

points.description: Arrow from the delocalised π ring to N of NO₂⁺
Intermediate: one sp³ carbon with H and NO₂; positive charge delocalised over the other five carbons
Arrow from the C–H bond into the ring; H⁺ lost and delocalisation restored (H⁺ + HSO₄⁻ → H₂SO₄)

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: A curly arrow goes from the delocalised π electrons to the nitrogen of NO₂⁺. The intermediate cation has one sp³ carbon carrying H and NO₂, with the positive charge spread over the remaining five carbons. A curly arrow from the C–H bond back into the ring restores the aromatic system and H⁺ is lost; it reforms H₂SO₄ with HSO₄⁻.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Why does the intermediate lose H⁺ instead of adding a nucleophile?

options.content: No nucleophiles are present in the nitrating mixture.
The intermediate is negatively charged and repels nucleophiles.
Adding a nucleophile would form a free radical.
Loss of H⁺ restores the stable delocalised ring.
options.rationale: Correct: addition would lose the delocalisation energy.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Calculate the percentage yield, to one decimal place. Ar: H 1.0, C 12.0, N 14.0, O 16.0.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: Above about 60 °C a second nitro group is substituted. Name the main product.

parts.label: (g)
parts.stem: Sulfuric acid is regenerated at the end of the mechanism and acts as a catalyst.

explanation: NO₂⁺; electrophilic substitution via a cation with charge over five carbons; yield 70.7%; 1,3-dinitrobenzene at higher temperature.
hints: The ring donates electrons to NO₂⁺.

stem:
Methylbenzene reacts with chlorine in two different ways:

| Reaction | Conditions | Organic product(s) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Cl₂, AlCl₃ catalyst, room temperature, dark | two ring-substituted isomers |
| 2 | Cl₂, ultraviolet light, no catalyst | C₆H₅CH₂Cl |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: What type of reaction is reaction 2?

options.content: electrophilic substitution
nucleophilic substitution
electrophilic addition
options.rationale: Nothing adds to a double bond.

options.content: free-radical substitution

parts.explanation: Cl• radicals abstract a side-chain hydrogen.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Name the two products of reaction 1.

points.description: 2-chloromethylbenzene
4-chloromethylbenzene

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Methylbenzene is heated under reflux with alkaline KMnO₄ and the mixture is then acidified. Name the organic product.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Calculate the maximum mass, in g, of this product from 2.30 g of methylbenzene. Ar: H 1.0, C 12.0, O 16.0.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: The product of reaction 2 gives a white precipitate when warmed with ethanolic silver nitrate, but the products of reaction 1 do not. Explain this difference.

points.description: In C₆H₅CH₂Cl the Cl is on a side-chain (sp³) carbon, so it behaves like a halogenoalkane and is hydrolysed, releasing Cl⁻ (AgCl white)
In the ring compounds a Cl lone pair overlaps with the delocalised π system, giving the C–Cl bond partial double-bond character (stronger)
and the π electrons repel the nucleophile, so the C–Cl bond is not broken and no Cl⁻ forms

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: In (chloromethyl)benzene the chlorine is bonded to a side-chain carbon, so the C–Cl bond is an ordinary halogenoalkane bond that is hydrolysed, releasing chloride ions that give white AgCl. In the chloromethylbenzenes from reaction 1 the chlorine is bonded to the ring; a chlorine lone pair is delocalised into the ring, giving the C–Cl bond partial double-bond character so it is stronger, and the ring's π electrons repel nucleophiles, so no hydrolysis occurs.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: Methylbenzene reacts with electrophiles faster than benzene does.

explanation: Reaction 2 is free-radical substitution; reaction 1 gives 2- and 4-chloromethylbenzene; benzoic acid 3.05 g; ring C–Cl resists hydrolysis.
hints: Catalyst in the dark → ring; UV → side chain.

stem: 3-bromo-3-methylhexane, CH₃CH₂C(CH₃)BrCH₂CH₂CH₃, is chiral. A pure enantiomer of it is hydrolysed by aqueous hydroxide ions to 3-methylhexan-3-ol, CH₃CH₂C(CH₃)(OH)CH₂CH₂CH₃.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: How many chiral centres are present in 3-methylhexan-3-ol?
parts.explanation: C3 carries OH, CH₃, C₂H₅ and C₃H₇.
parts.workedSolution: 1. C3 carries OH, CH₃, C₂H₅ and C₃H₇.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Describe how the two optical isomers of 3-methylhexan-3-ol are related.

points.description: The four different groups are arranged tetrahedrally around C3
The isomers are mirror images that cannot be superimposed (enantiomers)

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Both have OH, CH₃, C₂H₅ and C₃H₇ arranged tetrahedrally around C3; the two arrangements are mirror images and are non-superimposable.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: The alcohol formed is optically inactive. Which statement explains this?

options.content: The halogenoalkane reacts by SN2, which always gives an inactive product.
options.rationale: SN2 gives a single inverted enantiomer.

options.content: It reacts by SN1 via a planar carbocation, giving a racemic mixture.
options.rationale: Correct: the carbocation is attacked equally from both sides.

options.content: The product molecule has no chiral centre.
options.rationale: C3 of the product is chiral.

options.content: The hydroxide ion is chiral and cancels the rotation.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Give the name for a 50 : 50 mixture of two enantiomers.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: A single enantiomer of 2-bromohexane is hydrolysed under conditions where only SN2 occurs. Predict and explain the optical activity of the product.

points.description: The product (hexan-2-ol) is optically active: a single enantiomer forms
SN2 is one step with backside attack, inverting the configuration rather than forming a planar intermediate

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The product is optically active. In SN2 the nucleophile attacks from the side opposite the bromine in a single step, so the configuration is inverted and only one enantiomer of hexan-2-ol forms.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: Many drugs are chiral. Suggest why a manufacturer may choose to make a drug as a single enantiomer rather than as a racemic mixture.

points.description: The other enantiomer may be inactive or have harmful side effects (it fits receptors differently)
A smaller dose is needed / less waste / fewer side effects

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The two enantiomers fit chiral receptors differently, so one may be inactive or harmful; supplying only the active enantiomer allows a smaller dose with fewer side effects.

parts.label: (g)
parts.stem: The two enantiomers of 3-methylhexan-3-ol have the same boiling point.
parts.explanation: Enantiomers have identical physical properties apart from optical rotation.

explanation: One chiral centre; SN1 gives a racemate; SN2 gives a single inverted enantiomer; single-enantiomer drugs avoid inactive or harmful isomers.
